artiest/afrika-bambaataa-en-the-soulsoni.text:
Afrika Bambaataa, born Lance Taylor in 1957 in the Bronx, was an American DJ, rapper and producer. He grew up in the Bronx River Projects and became a member of the street gang the Black Spades. After a trip to Africa, which he won in an essay competition, he took his name from a Zulu leader and built up the Universal Zulu Nation, an organisation centred on music and culture that was meant to get young people off the street. He held parties in the South Bronx and was known as the Master of Records.

Within that movement he formed rap groups, among them Soulsonic Force. In 1982 he released Planet Rock with them, together with producer Arthur Baker. The record blended drum machines and synthesizers with funk and hip hop, and used a synthesizer line from Kraftwerk's Trans-Europe Express. Planet Rock became a big hit in the clubs and went gold. It set off a whole current of electro, in which rap and electronics go together. Bambaataa named Kraftwerk and Yellow Magic Orchestra as sources of inspiration and gave up live bands on stage.

His role in the history of hip hop is great, but not uncontroversial. In 2016 he stepped down as leader of the Universal Zulu Nation following accusations of sexual abuse of minors. The music of Planet Rock shows how hip hop began to look to the future.
artiest/afrika-bambaataa-en-the-soulsoni.listen: Listen to Planet Rock and notice the electronic rhythms and synthesizers, and hear how the rappers talk over them in short, rhythmic phrases.

artiest/afrojack.text:
Afrojack is the stage name of Nick van de Wall, born in 1987 in Spijkenisse to a Dutch mother and a Surinamese father. He learned to play piano at five. After a year at the Grafisch Lyceum in Rotterdam he chose music. At fourteen he was already DJing in pubs and clubs and, alongside that, building websites for other musicians. In 2007 his first recording under the name Afrojack appeared, the single In Your Face, and he founded the label Wall Recordings.

His international breakthrough came in 2010 with Take Over Control, a collaboration with singer Eva Simons. The track charted in ten countries. In 2011 he contributed to Give Me Everything by Pitbull, with Ne-Yo and Nayer, and to Run the World (Girls) by Beyoncé. With David Guetta he won a Grammy for the remix of Revolver by Madonna. For years he ranked high in the DJ Mag Top 100 DJs and played festivals such as Tomorrowland, Ultra and Coachella. His debut album Forget the World followed in 2014.

His music is electronic dance music for big stages: hard, tight basses, a build-up to a drop and synthesizers that cut. Afrojack shows how Dutch DJs of the 2010s came to define global dance culture. Under the name NLW he has also been making rougher, more underground-sounding tracks since 2017.
artiest/afrojack.listen: Listen to Take Over Control and notice the build-up to the drop and how the voice of Eva Simons then contrasts with the hard synthesizer. Do you hear how little melody the beat needs?

artiest/aga-mayo-butocan.text:
Aga Mayo Butocan was a master of the kulintang, the music of the Maguindanao in the south of the Philippines. Kulintang is an ancient instrumental tradition. A row of small gongs lies horizontally on a frame and carries the melody. Larger hanging gongs and drums accompany. The player strikes the bosses of the gongs with two wooden sticks. Since the twentieth century a Maguindanao ensemble has usually consisted of five or six instruments.

This music belongs to the gong culture of Southeast Asia, alongside the gamelan of West Java and the piphat of Thailand, Burma, Cambodia and Laos. Kulintang is older than the influences of Hinduism, Buddhism, Islam, Christianity and the West. There are hardly any recorded sources about its origin.

Butocan played a key role in handing down that tradition. In 1968 the ethnomusicologist José Maceda at the University of the Philippines drew attention to her new interest in kulintang. Butocan devised a notation system and wrote Palabunibunyan, a collection of kulintang pieces from Maguindanao, which made the music easier to learn. She also stressed the improvised character of the playing. That made kulintang popular among students from all over the country. For a Western listener the sound takes some getting used to: bright and metallic, without chords, with repetition and variation instead of a build-up to a chorus.
artiest/aga-mayo-butocan.listen: Listen to Sinulog a Bagu and notice the gong playing in the foreground and the larger gongs and drums beneath it. Try to follow the rhythm in the low sounds while the high gongs play the melody.

artiest/agnetha-faltskog.text:
Agnetha Fältskog was born in 1950 in Jönköping in Sweden. At six she wrote her first song, after that she had piano lessons and sang in a church choir. At fifteen she left school, worked as a telephonist and sang in a dance band in the evenings. A broken heart inspired her to write Jag var så kär, her first single. At the beginning of 1968 that song was at number 1 in Sweden, and she grew into one of the most popular singers in the country, writing many of her own songs. In 1972 she played Mary Magdalene in the Swedish version of Jesus Christ Superstar.

In 1971 she married Björn Ulvaeus. Together with Benny Andersson and Anni-Frid Lyngstad they formed ABBA, the group of two couples that won the Eurovision Song Contest with Waterloo in 1974 and then had hits all over the world. Fältskog sang the lead part in many of the best-known songs, such as SOS, The Winner Takes It All, One of Us and The Day Before You Came. She and Ulvaeus divorced in 1980; their failed marriage inspired him to write the words of The Winner Takes It All. After ABBA she made solo albums such as Wrap Your Arms Around Me (1983), then withdrew for a long time. In 2021 the album Voyage appeared with ABBA after all.

Fältskog has a clear soprano voice with a wide range. She named Connie Francis, Aretha Franklin and Petula Clark as examples. It was precisely her voice that became, for many listeners, the sound of ABBA.
artiest/agnetha-faltskog.listen: Listen to The Winner Takes It All by ABBA and notice the voice of Agnetha Fältskog: clear and controlled, but full of emotion. Hear how the song keeps building, while the lyrics are about a divorce that she went through herself.

artiest/ahmad-balshe.text:
Ahmad Balshe, known as an artist under the name Belly, is a Palestinian-Canadian rapper, singer, songwriter and producer. He was born in Jenin in 1984. When he was seven, his family fled violence and poverty via Saudi Arabia, Lebanon and Jordan to Ottawa in Canada, where he grew up. After a series of mixtapes his debut album The Revolution appeared in 2007, which won a Juno Award in Canada for best rap recording. On tracks such as History of Violence he rapped about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and the war in Iraq.

From 2011 Balshe co-wrote music for his fellow Canadian The Weeknd. He has credits on all of his studio albums, including six tracks on Beauty Behind the Madness (2015), such as The Hills and Earned It, and nine on Starboy (2016). In 2015 he signed as an artist to The Weeknd's label XO. His mixtape Up for Days, with the single Might Not, came out on XO and Roc Nation. For the album After Hours (2020) he co-wrote Blinding Lights, which Billboard declared in 2021 to be the greatest Hot 100 hit of all time. His own albums Immigrant (2018) and See You Next Wednesday (2021) followed, and 96 Miles from Bethlehem (2024) is about what it means to be Palestinian.

Balshe is an example of the behind-the-scenes writers who help shape today's big hits. Blinding Lights has five writers, including Max Martin; Balshe is one of them. He also sang on and co-wrote 6 Inch by Beyoncé, and in 2016 he was named songwriter of the year in Canada.
artiest/ahmad-balshe.listen: Listen to Blinding Lights by The Weeknd and notice how the track is built: a driving synthesizer riff and a beat that recall the 1980s. Bear in mind that five writers worked on this song: do you hear how tightly every part falls into place?

artiest/ahmad-jamal.text:
Ahmad Jamal was an American jazz pianist, composer and bandleader. He was born Frederick Russell Jones in Pittsburgh in 1930. He began playing piano at three, had lessons at seven and at eleven was already playing études by Liszt. At fourteen he played professionally and Art Tatum called him a future great. In 1950 he moved to Chicago. Around that time he converted to Islam and took the name Ahmad Jamal.

He made his first records in 1951 with The Three Strings, a trio of piano, guitar and bass. After a performance in New York producer John Hammond signed him to Okeh. His big breakthrough came with the live album At the Pershing: But Not for Me, recorded in 1958 with bassist Israel Crosby and drummer Vernel Fournier. It spent 108 weeks in the bestseller chart. Poinciana on that album became his best-known track. In the 1960s he settled in New York, and later he also played electric piano.

Jamal played in an understated way, with a lot of space, a light touch and a strong sense of rhythm. Miles Davis said he was impressed by this, and had his own musicians listen to Jamal. In this way Jamal had a great influence on a Cool Jazz that used rhythm and silence as an instrument. He later received a Grammy for his life's work.
artiest/ahmad-jamal.listen: Listen to Poinciana from At the Pershing and notice the space between the notes and how the rhythm of bass and drums carries the piano.

artiest/ahn-sook-sun.text: Ahn Sook-sun from Namwon learned pansori from her aunt and, as a teenager, already knew the five classic stories, each of which lasts hours. In pansori a single singer sings, narrates and acts out an entire story, with only a drummer beside them. From the age of 31 she sang in the national changgeuk company, and in 1998 she performed at the Avignon festival. In Korea she is honoured as a living national treasure.
artiest/ahn-sook-sun.listen: Listen to the excerpt from Simcheongga: her voice is hoarse and powerful, and the drummer encourages her with short exclamations.

artiest/air.text: Air is a French duo from Versailles, formed in 1995 by Nicolas Godin and Jean-Benoît Dunckel. Godin studied architecture, Dunckel mathematics. Their debut album Moon Safari (1998) brought a soft, electronic pop sound with Moog synthesizers, vocoder, Wurlitzer and Rhodes piano. For Sofia Coppola's first feature film, The Virgin Suicides (1999), Air wrote a complete score. It appeared in 2000 as an album in its own right. Brian Reitzell played drums, and in Playground Love Thomas Mars of Phoenix sings under the name Gordon Tracks. The album was nominated for a Brit Award for best soundtrack. Later Air contributed to Coppola's Lost in Translation (2003) and made an album for Le voyage dans la lune (2012).
artiest/air.listen: Listen to the slow, dreamy chords on Rhodes and synthesizer, the languid drums and the saxophone, which evoke the bored summer of the film.

artiest/airto-moreira.text: Percussionist Airto Moreira grew up in the south of Brazil and played in Brazil in groups such as the Quarteto Novo. At the end of the 1960s he went to the United States with Flora Purim. Miles Davis took him into his band around 1970; after that he played in the first line-up of Weather Report and of Return to Forever. Airto brought Brazilian percussion instruments such as the cuíca, the berimbau and all kinds of shakers into jazz. He is often cited as the one who gave the percussionist a permanent place in the jazz band. Fingers (1972) shows his own music.
artiest/airto-moreira.listen: Seek out the small percussion sounds: each little sound has a place of its own.

artiest/akino-arai.text:
Akino Arai is a Japanese singer, songwriter and lyricist, born in 1959 in Tokyo. She is best known for music for anime. After her studies she went to work at Victor Music Entertainment. In 1986 her first single Yakusoku appeared, which was used in the anime Windaria, along with her first album Natsukashii Mirai. In 1988 she left her record company.

In the 1990s she returned with music for series and film. In 1992 she sang songs for Record of Lodoss War. In 1994 she sang Voices for Macross Plus, in which she was also the singing voice of two characters. Her first compilation album, Sora no Mori, appeared in 1997. Outlaw Star in 1998 and Spice and Wolf II in 2009 followed, among others. In 2005 she celebrated her twentieth anniversary with the compilation album Sora no Uta. A year later she toured France and Germany, and in 2013 she gave her first concert in Asia outside Japan. She also collaborated with other artists and was in groups such as Marsh-mallow and RuRu Chapeau.

She also presented a weekly radio programme, Viridian House. Her music shows how anime music can build a world of its own out of song, atmosphere and story, and how important Japanese lyricists are in that for an international audience.
artiest/akino-arai.listen: Listen to Voices and notice how the singing carries the melody and what atmosphere the music around it builds up.

artiest/akira-ifukube.text: Akira Ifukube (1914–2006) came from Hokkaido and taught himself to compose while working as a forestry scientist. The music of the Ainu and Japanese folk music formed his sound world. For Gojira (1954) he had little time. He wrote a heavy, repetitive march for low brass and strings, which gave the monster the weight of a natural disaster. He also devised Godzilla's roar: a leather glove rubbed with resin, drawn along the strings of a double bass. That march returned in many later Godzilla films, such as Mosura tai Gojira (1964). He also scored serious dramas such as Biruma no tategoto (1956) and taught many Japanese composers.
artiest/akira-ifukube.listen: Notice the stubborn ostinatos in the low register, which are repeated again and again without really developing, and the dissonant brass chords.

artiest/akira-sakata.text:
Akira Sakata is a Japanese free jazz saxophonist, born in 1945 in Kure near Hiroshima. He first heard jazz on shortwave radio and through Voice of America, and became more interested in it through film music. At secondary school he played clarinet. At Hiroshima University he played alto saxophone in a jazz band. He studied to become a marine biologist and moved to Tokyo in 1969.

From 1972 to 1979 he played in the Yamashita Yosuke Trio, with which he toured internationally. In 1986 he played with Last Exit and Bill Laswell. That performance appeared as The Noise of Trouble: Live in Tokyo. Laswell later played bass on albums by Sakata and produced them, such as Mooko, Silent Plankton and Fisherman's.com. The guitarist Pete Cosey, who had worked with Miles Davis, also played on the last of these. Sakata also collaborated with DJ Krush and with Chikamorachi. In 2002 he suffered a brain haemorrhage. He had to learn to play the saxophone again and performed again after three months.

Sakata is also an actor for television and film, and a writer. He has invented a language of his own, which Japanese people find very funny. On stage he sometimes puts his saxophone down and makes sounds only with his voice, which is both funny and musical. In this way he shows that free jazz does not have to sound serious all the time.
artiest/akira-sakata.listen: Listen to a recording by Sakata, for example from Fisherman.com, and notice how freely he handles tone and rhythm.

artiest/al-di-meola.text:
Al Di Meola is an American guitarist, born in 1954 in Jersey City and raised in Bergenfield, New Jersey. He began playing guitar at eight after hearing Elvis Presley and the Ventures. Meet the Beatles! then decided that he wanted to be a musician. As a teenager he practised eight to ten hours a day. He studied at the Berklee College of Music in 1971 and at nineteen was asked by Chick Corea to join Return to Forever, in place of Bill Connors.

He played in that band for a few years with Stanley Clarke and Lenny White. Three albums with him reached the American top forty, and Romantic Warrior appeared in 1976. When Corea disbanded the group, Di Meola began his solo career. Land of the Midnight Sun came out in 1976 and Elegant Gypsy in 1977, followed by Casino in 1978 and Splendido Hotel in 1980. Later he made the World Sinfonia albums and Di Meola Plays Piazzolla, among others. He collaborated with Paco de Lucía, John McLaughlin, Jaco Pastorius and Paul Simon, and won a Grammy.

His music is known for technical mastery, complex compositions and Latin American influences. He brought the fast electric guitar of fusion closer to world music, flamenco and tango. In terms of pop history he shows how jazz and rock came together in the 1970s.
artiest/al-di-meola.listen: Listen to Elegant Gypsy and notice the lightning-fast guitar playing and the Latin influences in rhythm and melody.

artiest/al-dubin.text:
Al Dubin was an American lyricist, born in 1891 in Zürich to a Russian-Jewish family that moved to the United States. He grew up in Philadelphia. As a teenager he played truant to see Broadway shows in New York, and at fourteen he was already writing songs for a vaudeville performer in Tin Pan Alley. In 1911 he wrote Oh, You, Mister Moon with Joe Burke. In 1917 he was called up for the army and wrote a song there for his division. In 1921 he became a member of ASCAP.

In 1925 he met Harry Warren, the composer with whom he later worked at Warner Bros. in Hollywood. That same year he had his first big hit with Joseph Meyer, A Cup of Coffee, a Sandwich and You. From 1932 he officially formed a team with Warren for the film musical 42nd Street. Between 1932 and 1939 they wrote sixty hits for Warners musicals, including for Gold Diggers of 1933, Footlight Parade, Dames and Wonder Bar. Lullaby of Broadway from Gold Diggers of 1935 won an Oscar for best song in 1936.

Dubin was a striking and exuberant personality, but in the 1940s he struggled with alcohol and drugs and hardly worked any more. He died in 1945. His lyrics for Hollywood musicals are an important part of the American songbook tradition, and the 1980 Broadway version of 42nd Street used his songs again.
artiest/al-dubin.listen: Listen to Lullaby of Broadway in a version from the film and notice how the words follow the rhythm of the music and paint a small scene.

artiest/al-green.text:
Al Green is an American soul singer, songwriter and preacher, born in 1946 in Forrest City, Arkansas. He began singing with his sister as a child. The family moved to Grand Rapids in Michigan. At secondary school he started a vocal group, which had the hit Back Up Train in 1966. The producer Willie Mitchell heard him and brought him to Hi Records in Memphis in 1969.

With Mitchell and the Hi Rhythm Section Green had his greatest successes. Let's Stay Together from 1972 was his best-known song and topped the Billboard Hot 100 and the R&B chart. In the same period came I'm Still in Love With You in 1972, Call Me in 1973 and Livin' for You in 1973. Love and Happiness and Take Me to the River were also radio hits. The latter was later covered by Talking Heads. In 1979 he fell off the stage in Cincinnati, which he took as a sign from God. He became a preacher and recorded gospel albums in the 1980s, such as The Lord Will Make a Way in 1980.

His voice moves between soft whispering and sharp flights, and the band around him plays in a restrained, warm way. He has been inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and won eleven Grammys. He is known as one of the great voices of Memphis soul.
artiest/al-green.listen: Listen to Let's Stay Together and notice how softly he sings and how the band stays quietly beneath the voice.

artiest/al-haig.text:
Al Haig was an American jazz pianist and one of the pioneers of bebop. He was born in 1922 in Newark, New Jersey, and grew up in Nutley. In 1940 he studied piano at Oberlin College. From 1945 he played with Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker. He recorded with Gillespie until 1946, played in groups led by Eddie Davis in 1946 and 1947, and worked for Parker from 1948 to 1950 and for Stan Getz from 1949 to 1951.

The quintet of Gillespie with Haig recorded four sides in May 1945 for Guild Records, which are regarded as the first recordings with all the elements of the mature bebop style. Haig was also in the nonet at the first session of Birth of the Cool by Miles Davis. After that it went quiet around him. In the 1950s and 1960s he often played in bars and in music outside jazz, and critics said that his clear touch and quick, logical ideas no longer had a place in an increasingly percussive piano style.

In 1974 Tony Williams of Spotlite Records invited him on a tour of Europe. That led to Invitation, with Bibi Rovère and Kenny Clarke, and gave his career a new start. Until his death in 1982 he had a loyal audience in Europe and also recorded in Japan. His albums include Jazz Will-O-The-Wisp from 1957, Al in Paris from 1977 and Blue Manhattan from 1984. He shows what bebop sounds like on the piano.
artiest/al-haig.listen: Listen to a recording of Al Haig from his bebop years, and notice how the piano plays fast, clear lines alongside the horns.

artiest/al-jackson-jr.text:
Al Jackson Jr. was an American drummer, producer and songwriter from Memphis, born in 1935. His father led a jazz and swing dance orchestra, and at five the young Jackson was already playing in it. Later he drummed in the bands of trumpeter and producer Willie Mitchell and of Ben Branch. Keyboard player Booker T. Jones recommended him to the label Stax, and Jackson became the first session musician there on a fixed weekly wage.

At Stax, with Booker T. Jones, guitarist Steve Cropper and bassist Lewie Steinberg, later Duck Dunn, he formed the group Booker T. & the M.G.'s. As the house band they played on records by Otis Redding, Sam & Dave, Rufus and Carla Thomas, Eddie Floyd and Albert King, among others, and they also made instrumental tracks of their own. In the 1970s Jackson co-wrote and played on hits by Al Green, such as Let's Stay Together and I'm Still in Love with You, and drummed for artists such as Aretha Franklin, Bill Withers and Elvis Presley. In 1975, shortly before a planned reunion of the M.G.'s, he was shot dead in his home in Memphis. The culprit was never found.

Jackson was nicknamed The Human Timekeeper, the human metronome. His playing was tight, simple and instantly recognisable: a steady backbeat that sat exactly right in the groove. In this way he gave the sound of Stax and southern soul its backbone, and he is regarded as one of the most influential drummers in the history of recorded music.
artiest/al-jackson-jr.listen: Listen to Let's Stay Together by Al Green and notice the drums of Al Jackson Jr.: calm, tight and without unnecessary embellishments. Hear how that simple, steady backbeat makes the whole song float.

artiest/al-jarreau.text:
Al Jarreau was an American singer from Milwaukee, where he was born in 1940. His father was a preacher and singer, his mother played piano in church, and the whole family sang together at church concerts. Jarreau studied psychology and first worked as a counsellor for people with disabilities in San Francisco. In the evenings he sang in a jazz trio led by pianist George Duke. With guitarist Julio Martinez he became the big draw of a small club in Sausalito, and in 1968 he chose music for good.

In 1975 his debut album We Got By came out, followed by Glow (1976). He won Grammys for both jazz and pop vocals, ten in total. His best-known album is Breakin' Away (1981), with We're in This Love Together and Roof Garden. That album is seen as one of the best examples of the smooth pop and R&B from Los Angeles of that time. Later he sang the title song of the TV series Moonlighting and a line in We Are the World.

Jarreau was nicknamed the acrobat of scat. He used his voice as an instrument: he sang fast lines without words, imitated drums and percussion with clicks and breath sounds, and leapt effortlessly from low to high. In this way he brought the technique of jazz singers to a large pop audience. He collaborated with Chick Corea, George Benson and Miles Davis, among others. He died in 2017.
artiest/al-jarreau.listen: Listen to Roof Garden from 1981. Notice the passages in which Jarreau sings without words and makes percussive sounds with his voice, as if he himself were an instrument in the band.

artiest/al-jolson.text:
Al Jolson was born Asa Yoelson around 1886 in a village near Kaunas in Lithuania, then still part of the Russian Empire. His father was a rabbi and cantor and took the family to New York in 1894. His mother died in 1895. As a boy he sang in the street with his brother for coins. Around 1902 he worked in a circus, then in vaudeville, and from 1911 he was a star on Broadway, at the Winter Garden Theatre in New York. In his revues he asked the audience for an extra song with the words that they had not heard anything yet.

In January 1920 he recorded Swanee, a song by the twenty-year-old George Gershwin. It was an instant enormous hit and made both the singer and the composer known in America and Europe. In those years Jolson was one of the best-paid stars in the United States. In 1927 he starred in The Jazz Singer, the first major film with spoken dialogue, and in the 1930s a series of musical films followed. After the attack on Pearl Harbor he was the first star to entertain troops overseas. The 1946 film The Jolson Story brought back his popularity.

His style was extravagant, sentimental and full of energy. He took his repertoire from Black music and brought it to a white audience. This was done in blackface, a tradition that confirmed racist stereotypes. That makes his legacy difficult: he was a pioneer of modern show business, but his act cannot be separated from that practice. He died in 1950.
artiest/al-jolson.listen: Listen to Swanee and notice the exuberant way of singing, full of emphasis and feeling. Hear how the singer seems to talk to the audience and does not merely recite a melody.

artiest/al-lucas.text:
Al Lucas was a Canadian jazz double bassist. As a child he had piano lessons from his mother, a concert pianist, and at twelve he switched to double bass and tuba. In 1933 he moved to New York. There he played first with Kaiser Marshall and then, from 1933 to 1942, with the Sunset Royal Serenaders. His year of birth is given differently in the sources, 1912 or 1916, but his career is clear.

In the 1940s he could be heard on records by Hot Lips Page, Coleman Hawkins, Eddie Heywood, Duke Ellington, Mary Lou Williams, James P. Johnson, J.J. Johnson, Ben Webster, Erroll Garner and Eddie South. From 1947 to 1953 he toured and recorded with Illinois Jacquet, including in Detroit with an all-star band. After that he played with Heywood again from 1954 to 1956. In the 1950s he also recorded with Ruby Braff, Charlie Byrd and Teddy Wilson.

Lucas was not a bandleader but a musician who supported others. He was the bassist who kept the rhythm and the chords in place, and he did that for many of the most important names in swing and bebop. In the last twenty years of his life he worked mainly as a studio musician, including at performances at the Apollo Theater, and only occasionally played jazz. He died in 1983 in New York. His name is thus on a remarkable number of records that shaped jazz history.
artiest/al-lucas.listen: Listen to a jazz recording from the 1940s on which Lucas plays and notice the double bass, which holds the beat and the chords.

artiest/al-martino.text:
Al Martino was an American singer of traditional pop and standards, born Jasper Cini in 1927 in Philadelphia. His father and grandfather came from Abruzzo in Italy. He wanted to become a singer after the example of Al Jolson and Perry Como, and of Mario Lanza, a friend of the family. After his service in the navy in the Second World War he took the name Al Martino and sang in nightclubs. In 1948 he moved to New York. In 1952 he won a talent contest on television.

His big hit was Here in My Heart from 1952, three weeks at number one in the United States and also the first number one of the British chart. At Capitol Records there followed Take My Heart, Rachel and When You're Mine, among others. Later he remained popular in England and Europe. In 1976 he had a big hit in several European countries with a disco version of Volare. In 1993 he made an album with Dieter Bohlen. Albums from his long career include I Love You Because from 1963, Spanish Eyes from 1966 and Love Theme From The Godfather from 1972.

In 1972 he played the singer Johnny Fontane in the film The Godfather and sang the theme Speak Softly Love. He played that role in the third part as well. His warm, round voice and his careful singing style make him one of the best-known Italian-American crooners. He died in 2009.
artiest/al-martino.listen: Listen to Here in My Heart and notice the long, smooth phrases with which he sings a love song, accompanied by an orchestra.

artiest/alan-civil.text:
Alan Civil was an English horn player, born in 1929. He began on the French horn at a young age and played as a teenager in the Royal Artillery Band in Woolwich. He had lessons from Aubrey Brain, the father of the famous horn player Dennis Brain, and later from Willy von Stemm in Hamburg. Conductor Thomas Beecham brought him to the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra, where he played second horn next to Dennis Brain and later led the horn section. In 1955 he went to the Philharmonia, where he became principal horn after Brain's death in 1957. From 1966 to 1988 he was principal horn of the BBC Symphony Orchestra.

As a soloist Civil recorded the horn concertos of Mozart with the Philharmonia under Otto Klemperer, and his recording of the Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings by Benjamin Britten with tenor Robert Tear became well known. He also played chamber music in his own Alan Civil Horn Trio and taught at the Royal College of Music. He died in 1989.

Outside the classical world Civil became known for his work with The Beatles. On For No One from the album Revolver he played the horn solo, and he was one of the few session musicians to be named on a Beatles record. He also played in the orchestra of A Day in the Life. His name thus shows how The Beatles brought in classical musicians in the studio to give their pop music new tone colours.
artiest/alan-civil.listen: Listen to For No One by The Beatles and notice the solo by Alan Civil on the French horn. Hear how that warm, classical sound stands out against the piano and the voice of Paul McCartney.

artiest/alan-howarth.text:
Alan Howarth is an American composer and sound designer who is best known for his work for Hollywood and for his collaboration with John Carpenter. He grew up in Cleveland, Ohio, and played in rock bands that opened for The Who and Cream. He then made his own music with synthesizers in the groups Braino and Pi Corp. From 1976 he did synthesizer work for the fusion band Weather Report, which led him to move to Los Angeles.

His big breakthrough came in 1980, when his music was used for the trailer of a Star Trek film. He then worked on the next five films in the series. With Carpenter he made music for Escape from New York, Halloween II, Halloween III: Season of the Witch, Christine, Big Trouble in Little China, Prince of Darkness and They Live. His sound designs can be heard in Raiders of the Lost Ark, Poltergeist, Back to the Future Part II and Total Recall. His team won Oscars for the sound of The Hunt for Red October and Bram Stoker's Dracula.

Howarth also plays his film music live to clips from the films, in Geneva, Kraków, New York and Paris, among other places. He also worked on multichannel surround sound, the forerunner of later systems such as Dolby Atmos. His work shows how the synthesizer in the 1980s defined the sound of the horror and science fiction film.
artiest/alan-howarth.listen: Listen to the music of Escape from New York and notice how the synthesizers build a menacing atmosphere with few notes.

artiest/alan-menken.text: Alan Menken (born in New York in 1949) began in the theatre. With lyricist Howard Ashman he wrote the musical Little Shop of Horrors, which was made into a film in 1986. Disney then brought the duo in. The Little Mermaid (1989), Beauty and the Beast (1991) and Aladdin (1992) brought the Broadway musical to the animated film, with a fixed type of song: the 'I want' song in which the main character tells what she longs for. This ushered in the so-called Disney Renaissance. Ashman died in 1991. Menken afterwards worked with other lyricists, such as Glenn Slater for Tangled (2010). He won eight Oscars.
artiest/alan-menken.listen: Listen to the theatrical build of the song: a quiet start, a chorus that builds and a musical climax that moves the story a step further.

artiest/alan-price.text:
Alan Price was born in 1942 in Fatfield in the north-English county of Durham. After school he worked as a tax clerk. He taught himself to play and founded the Alan Price Combo on Tyneside, a rhythm and blues group that later, when singer Eric Burdon joined, came to be called The Animals. Price played organ on the band's big hits, such as The House of the Rising Sun, Don't Let Me Be Misunderstood and Bring It On Home to Me.

In 1965 he left The Animals, officially because of a fear of flying, but also because of tensions in the group. A conflict over the royalties of The House of the Rising Sun, which went only to Price, played a part. With his new group, the Alan Price Set, he had hits with I Put a Spell on You (1966), Simon Smith and His Amazing Dancing Bear by the then unknown Randy Newman, and his own The House That Jack Built (1967). Later followed Rosetta with Georgie Fame (1971) and the autobiographical Jarrow Song (1974). He wrote the music for the film O Lucky Man! (1973) by Lindsay Anderson, for which he won a BAFTA, and acted in films himself.

Price was above all a pianist and organist, with a style that draws on rhythm and blues and jazz. His improvised organ solo in The House of the Rising Sun is one of the best-known moments in British beat music, and showed that the electric organ in a rock band could have a voice of its own.
artiest/alan-price.listen: Listen to The House of the Rising Sun by The Animals and notice the moment when Alan Price's electric organ begins its solo. Hear how the organ builds the tension, after which Eric Burdon's vocal goes to a climax.

artiest/alan-silva.text:
Alan Silva is an American free jazz musician, best known as a double bassist. He was born in 1939 in Bermuda as a British subject, with an Azorean-Portuguese mother and a Black Bermudian father. At five he emigrated with his mother to the United States and grew up in Harlem in New York. He began on trumpet and switched to the upright bass. He took his stage name in his twenties. In 1988 he said that he had always continued to feel Bermudian.

Silva is regarded as one of the most inventive bassists in jazz. He played with well-known names from the avant-garde, such as Cecil Taylor, Sun Ra, Albert Ayler, Sunny Murray and Archie Shepp. In 1964 he took part in October Revolution in Jazz, a pioneering gathering of free jazz, and in 1967 in the live album Albert Ayler in Greenwich Village. Since the early 1970s he has lived mainly in Paris. There he founded the Celestrial Communication Orchestra, a group for free jazz in changing line-ups. In the 1980s he started a music school with two others, the I.A.C.P., which was intended as a jazz conservatoire.

In the 1990s he began playing electronic keyboards, because his bass playing no longer surprised him. He also used electric violin and electric sarangi. Around 2000 he again performed more often as a bassist and bandleader, including at the Vision Festival in New York. His albums include Skilfullness from 1969 and The Ongoing Strings from 1981.
artiest/alan-silva.listen: Listen to Albert Ayler in Greenwich Village and notice how the double bass there does not merely keep time, but improvises along in the free interplay.

artiest/alan-silvestri.text: Alan Silvestri (born in New York in 1950) began as a jazz guitarist and in the 1970s wrote music for the police series CHiPs. Robert Zemeckis asked him for Romancing the Stone (1984), and afterwards for almost all of his films. In Back to the Future (1985) a large orchestra is heard with a heroic brass fanfare, which gives the journey through time an adventurous feel. Predator (1987), by contrast, has hard, rhythmic percussion. For Forrest Gump (1994) he wrote a simple piano theme that goes with the floating feather. Later he became the composer of the big Avengers films, such as Avengers: Endgame (2019).
artiest/alan-silvestri.listen: Notice the broad brass fanfares and the fast, driving strings that propel the action forward.

artiest/alan-tarney.text:
Alan Tarney is an English producer, songwriter and musician, born in 1945 in Workington. He spent his teenage years in Adelaide, Australia. There he met drummer Trevor Spencer, with whom he would collaborate for years. In 1967 he played bass in James Taylor Move, one of Australia's first psychedelic rock bands. In 1969 he moved to England, where he became a session musician and songwriter. From 1973 to 1977 he was a member of The Shadows.

The big breakthrough came in 1979. Tarney wrote and arranged We Don't Talk Anymore for Cliff Richard, which reached number 1 in England. He then produced Richard's albums I'm No Hero (1980) and Wired for Sound (1981), and hits such as January February by Barbara Dickson and More Than I Can Say by Leo Sayer. His sound was clear and melodic, with tight arrangements that fitted radio perfectly.

In the mid-1980s he began working with the Norwegian band A-ha. The first version of their single Take On Me, made with Tony Mansfield, failed to catch on. Tarney recorded the song again with the band and that version became a worldwide hit. He co-produced the debut album Hunting High and Low (1985) and produced Scoundrel Days (1986) and Stay on These Roads (1988). Later he also worked with Squeeze, The Dream Academy and Pulp. Tarney shows how much a producer can mean: the same song can, in other hands, be a flop or a classic.
artiest/alan-tarney.listen: Listen to Take On Me by A-ha in the version that Tarney produced. Notice the clear little synthesizer riff at the beginning and the vocal that climbs higher and higher in the chorus.

artiest/alanis-morissette.text:
Alanis Morissette is a Canadian-American singer and songwriter, born in 1974 in Ottawa. She began her career in Canada in the early 1990s with two dance-pop albums, Alanis in 1991 and Now Is the Time in 1992. She then moved to Los Angeles and made Jagged Little Pill, which came out in 1995. That album caught on worldwide and grew into one of the best-selling albums ever. She won five Grammys with it, including Album of the Year, and was at that time the youngest winner in that category.

With Supposed Former Infatuation Junkie from 1998 she chose a more experimental sound. That year her song Uninvited from the film City of Angels won two Grammys. From 2002 she produced herself, first Under Rug Swept, and later came So-Called Chaos, Flavors of Entanglement, Havoc and Bright Lights, Such Pretty Forks in the Road and The Storm Before the Calm, among others. Singles such as You Oughta Know, Hand in My Pocket, Ironic and Thank U were hits in large parts of the world. In 2019 Jagged Little Pill received a Broadway adaptation.

Her music is alternative rock with an emotional mezzo-soprano and a confessional way of writing. In the 1990s she became a symbol of feelings that women in pop music dared to express openly. She stands in pop history as one of the defining voices of the alternative rock of that time.
artiest/alanis-morissette.listen: Listen to You Oughta Know and notice how her voice shifts between restrained singing and outburst, and how the band builds the tension.

artiest/alban-berg.text:
Alban Berg was born in 1885 in Vienna and lived there all his life. He began composing at fifteen. Between 1904 and 1911 he had lessons from Arnold Schoenberg, who belonged to the Second Viennese School. His father died in 1900, after which the family fell into financial difficulty. Berg moved in the cultural elite of Vienna around 1900, with painters, writers and architects such as Gustav Klimt, Karl Kraus and Adolf Loos. In 1913 a concert with his Altenberg Lieder led to a riot, the notorious Skandalkonzert.

His best-known works are the operas Wozzeck, completed in 1922 and first performed in Berlin in 1925, and Lulu, on which he worked from 1928 and which was completed after his death. He also wrote the Lyric Suite from 1926, the Kammerkonzert and a violin concerto, written in 1935, the year of his death. Berg died of blood poisoning on 24 December 1935. The violin concerto bears the subtitle Dem Andenken eines Engels.

Berg combined the Romantic lyricism of Mahler with the twelve-tone technique of Schoenberg. His music is therefore regarded as more human and more emotional than that of his teacher. He left behind a relatively small body of work, but is regarded as one of the most important composers of the twentieth century. That is due to his expressive style, which connects atonality and feeling without the listener needing to know the theory.
artiest/alban-berg.listen: Listen to the beginning of the Andante from the Violin Concerto and notice how the soloist enters softly and singingly. Try to hear how tragic and yet lyrical the melody sounds, despite the twelve-tone technique.

artiest/albert-ammons.text:
Albert Ammons was an American pianist and one of the great names of boogie-woogie, a blues style that was popular from the late 1930s to the mid-1940s. He was born in 1907 in Chicago to two pianists. His interest in the style came from his friendship with Meade Lux Lewis and from his father's interest. Together they practised at home on the piano. In the 1920s he worked as a taxi driver, like Lewis, and the two played at parties. In 1934 he started his own band at Club DeLisa.

In 1936 he recorded with Albert Ammons's Rhythm Kings for Decca. Their version of Swanee River Boogie became a million-seller, and Boogie Woogie Stomp from the same year is regarded as the first boogie based on twelve bars, which was imitated by many jazz bands. He then went to New York and played with Pete Johnson at Café Society. On 23 December 1938 he appeared with Johnson and Lewis at Carnegie Hall, in John Hammond's concert From Spirituals to Swing, which fuelled the boogie-woogie craze. Two weeks later Alfred Lion, who had been there, recorded nine solos by him and began Blue Note Records with them.

His style revolves around a firm rhythm in the left hand and a playful right hand. In 1941 his music was used for a short animated film, Boogie-Doodle. He died in 1949. His son Gene Ammons became a tenor saxophonist.
artiest/albert-ammons.listen: Listen to Boogie Woogie Stomp and notice the unshakeable pattern of the left hand while the right hand plays variations over it.

artiest/albert-ammons-en-his-rhythm-king.text:
Albert Ammons was born in 1907 in Chicago, the son of two pianists. At ten he could already play. His interest in boogie-woogie, a blues style on the piano, arose through his friendship with Meade Lux Lewis and through his father's fondness for that style. In the 1920s he worked as a taxi driver, like Lewis, and the two played together at parties in clubs. In 1934 he started a group of his own at Club DeLisa, where he stayed for two years.

In 1936 he recorded for Decca as Albert Ammons's Rhythm Kings, a five-piece group. Swanee River Boogie became a million-seller with the Rhythm Kings. His recording of Boogie Woogie Stomp from the same year has been described as the first twelve-bar piano record. He then moved to New York and played with pianist Pete Johnson at Café Society. In December 1938 Ammons, Johnson and Lewis appeared at Carnegie Hall in From Spirituals to Swing, a concert by John Hammond that helped start the boogie-woogie craze. Alfred Lion, who was in the hall, started Blue Note Records shortly afterwards and recorded nine solo pieces by Ammons.

His playing rests on a pulsing left hand that repeats a fixed pattern, while the right hand plays and improvises above it. Ammons died in 1949, aged 42. His influence can be heard in pianists such as Jerry Lee Lewis, Dr. John and Erroll Garner, and so a line runs from the Chicago clubs to rock and roll.
artiest/albert-ammons-en-his-rhythm-king.listen: Listen to Boogie Woogie Stomp and notice the pianist's left hand, which keeps repeating the same pattern. Try to hear how the right hand plays on top of it and the band keeps going behind.

artiest/albert-ayler.text: Tenor saxophonist Albert Ayler from Cleveland played rhythm and blues and in an army band as a young man. In the early 1960s he played in Sweden and Denmark, still in the style of Sonny Rollins. In New York in 1964 he recorded Spiritual Unity for the small label ESP-Disk, with bassist Gary Peacock and drummer Sunny Murray. Ayler played with an enormous tone and a broad vibrato, and his themes resembled folk songs, marches and hymns. After that the group improvised freely and loudly. John Coltrane admired him and made sure that Impulse! gave him a contract. In November 1970 Ayler was found dead in the East River.
artiest/albert-ayler.listen: Listen to the simple theme, like a nursery rhyme, and how it then falls apart.

artiest/albert-ayler-trio.text:
Albert Ayler was born in 1936 in Cleveland, Ohio, and grew up in Shaker Heights. His father, a semi-professional saxophonist and violinist, taught him to play alto saxophone. Together they played duets in church, and that background deeply coloured his music. As a teenager he played in a rhythm and blues band and knew the bebop repertoire so well that he was nicknamed Little Bird. In the army he switched to tenor saxophone. In 1962 he moved to Sweden, where his recording career began, and in 1963 he settled in New York.

In 1964 he recorded the album Spiritual Unity for the young label ESP-Disk, the first jazz album on that label. He played in a trio with bassist Gary Peacock and drummer Sunny Murray. Bells and Spirits Rejoice in 1965 followed, among others. Ayler joined in the free improvisation of John Coltrane and Ornette Coleman, but went further: it was not only harmony and melody but also tone colour that carried the music. His melodies are simple, almost like folk songs or military marches, and they are played with a big, trembling tone. Critics find his style hard to classify as free jazz.

Ayler died in 1970, aged 34. His work influenced later generations of improvisers who saw the sound of the saxophone itself as music.
artiest/albert-ayler-trio.listen: Listen to Ghosts: First Variation and notice the simple, almost childlike melody with which the saxophone begins. Hear how it is then broken open by the improvisation and comes back again.

artiest/albert-prejean.text:
Albert Préjean was born in 1894 in Paris. He served in the First World War and received the Croix de Guerre for it and later the Legion of Honour. As an actor he made his first five films between 1921 and 1923 with director Henri Diamant-Berger. His roles were often those of the strong, generous hero of the common people.

His lasting fame comes from the films of René Clair, in the transition from silent film to sound film. These include the farce Un Chapeau de Paille d'Italie from 1927 and Sous les toits de Paris from 1930. In that last film the public heard him as a singer and the title song became a sales success for the new sound film. In 1929 he himself directed a medium-length film, L'Aventure de Luna-Park. In the 1930s he was also a popular singer, notably of La Valse de Dédé Montmartre.

He continued to make films during the Second World War as well. In 1942 he travelled with a group of French actors, at the invitation of the Germans, to film studios in Berlin. In 1979 a book of his memoirs appeared, written with the help of his son Patrick, a voice actor. He died that year.

Préjean shows how in France sound film gave the chanson a new platform: an actor could turn a street song into a national sound.
artiest/albert-prejean.listen: Listen to Sous les toits de Paris and notice the simple waltz melody and how the singer almost speaks. The song sounds like a street song from Paris.

artiest/alemu-aga.text: Alemu Aga from Entoto near Addis Ababa is a master of the begena, a large lyre with ten strings that in Ethiopia is called the harp of King David. He learned to play from his neighbour, the begena master Aleqa Tessema. The begena accompanies neither dance nor feast, but personal prayer and reflection. His album The Harp of King David appeared in 1994 in the Éthiopiques series.
artiest/alemu-aga.listen: Listen to Abatatchin Hoy and notice the buzzing of the strings: it comes from leather tabs against which the strings vibrate.

artiest/alessandro-alessandroni.text:
Alessandro Alessandroni was an Italian musician and composer, born in 1925. He played many instruments, including guitar, mandolin, sitar, accordion and piano, and was best known for his whistling technique. He wrote more than forty film scores and countless pieces of library music, music that is issued for use in film and television. He had been a friend of Ennio Morricone since his youth.

He worked with Morricone on several spaghetti Western soundtracks. Morricone often wrote for these with an unusual combination of instruments, voices and whistling. Alessandroni's twangy guitar riff is the heart of the main theme of The Good, the Bad and the Ugly. He also whistles on the soundtracks of Sergio Leone, including the Dollars trilogy and Once Upon a Time in the West. In 1961 he founded the eight-voice vocal ensemble I Cantori Moderni, with his wife Giulia De Mutiis among others. They sang wordless vocals on Italian films. The best known is Mah Nà Mah Nà, written by Piero Umiliani for a 1968 film and later made famous by The Muppet Show. He also founded the rock band Braen's Machine, together with Umiliani.

His own albums ranged from Fischio In Armonia from 1970 to Guitar Poetry from 1981. He also wrote film music for Lady Frankenstein and Killer Nun, among others. His whistling and guitar have become the sound of the spaghetti Western, and thereby part of the memory of film music.
artiest/alessandro-alessandroni.listen: Listen to the main theme of The Good, the Bad and the Ugly and notice the twangy guitar and the whistling that together carry the melody.

artiest/alessandro-cicognini.text: Alessandro Cicognini, born in Pescara, was Vittorio De Sica's regular composer. He wrote the music for the great films of Italian neorealism: Sciuscià (1946), Ladri di biciclette (1948), Miracolo a Milano (1951) and Umberto D. (1952). Those films showed ordinary life after the war, often with amateur actors in the street. Cicognini did not opt for a sober approach. He wrote melodic, Romantic orchestral music with a clear sentiment. That gave the harsh stories a human warmth. He also worked for popular comedies, such as the Don Camillo films, and for De Sica's Stazione Termini (1953).
artiest/alessandro-cicognini.listen: Notice the warm, singing melodies in the strings that give the poverty on screen an emotional colour.

artiest/alex-james.text:
Alex James is an English bassist, born in 1968 in Bournemouth. He got into music when he was at home with chickenpox in 1980, the week John Lennon was shot. He watched the Beatles film Help! over and over, bought a songbook and a guitar and began working out chords. At secondary school he was already playing in bands.

In 1988 James studied French at Goldsmiths College in London. There he met guitarist Graham Coxon, and through him Damon Albarn and Dave Rowntree. In 1989 he joined their new band Seymour, which soon came to be called Blur. With Blur he became one of the faces of Britpop: a group that joined English pop history, guitars and irony together. After a long break the band played together again in 2009, including at Glastonbury, and in 2012 Blur gave a concert in Hyde Park at the closing of the Olympic Games.

Besides Blur, James kept seeking other paths. In 1998 he formed Fat Les with actor Keith Allen and artist Damien Hirst; their football song Vindaloo became a big hit. He co-wrote and co-produced tracks by Sophie Ellis-Bextor and Marianne Faithfull, and played bass in Bad Lieutenant, the band of Bernard Sumner of New Order. Later he also became known as a radio presenter, writer and cheesemaker on his farm in Oxfordshire. His story shows how a Britpop musician grew into a versatile English public figure.
artiest/alex-james.listen: Listen to Girls & Boys by Blur. Notice Alex James's bass guitar: a driving, danceable line that pushes the song forward beneath the synthesizers and the vocals of Damon Albarn.

artiest/alex-north.text: Alex North studied at Juilliard and in Moscow and first wrote music for theatre and dance. Elia Kazan took him to Hollywood for A Streetcar Named Desire (1951). That was one of the first Hollywood scores to lean heavily on jazz and blues. The music follows the psyche of the characters instead of the action. Later North wrote big, modern epics such as Spartacus (1960) and Cleopatra (1963), with sharp dissonances and unusual instruments. For 2001: A Space Odyssey he wrote a score that Stanley Kubrick did not use. North was nominated fifteen times for an Oscar and received an honorary Oscar in 1986.
artiest/alex-north.listen: Notice the bluesy clarinet and saxophone in Streetcar and the hard, modern harmonies in Spartacus.

artiest/alex-turner.text:
Alex Turner is an English singer, songwriter and guitarist, the frontman of the rock band Arctic Monkeys. He was born in 1986 in Sheffield and grew up in the High Green district, the only child of two teachers. His father taught music and was a fan of jazz and swing. His mother played Led Zeppelin, David Bowie and the Eagles. From the age of five he grew up next to the boy next door, Matt Helders, with whom he later formed the band. At sixteen he founded Arctic Monkeys with three friends.

In 2005 the band attracted national attention, and their debut album Whatever People Say I Am, That's What I'm Not from 2006 became the fastest-selling debut album in British history. Favourite Worst Nightmare followed in 2007 and Humbug in 2009, for the first time with producer Josh Homme. After that came AM in 2013, among others, which is on Rolling Stone's list of the best albums of all time. The band tried out desert rock, indie pop, R&B and lounge. With Miles Kane he founded The Last Shadow Puppets in 2007. In 2010 he made the acoustic soundtrack album for the film Submarine.

Turner is known for his lyrics, which range from everyday realism to surreal wordplay. He has won seven Brit Awards and a Mercury Prize. In this way he has become a defining voice for British guitar music of the 2000s and beyond, a singer who could tell of ordinary life in an English city as a poet.
artiest/alex-turner.listen: Listen to a track from Whatever People Say I Am, That's What I'm Not and notice how Turner sings his lyrics over the fast guitars.

artiest/alexander-borodin.text:
Alexander Borodin was a Russian composer and chemist of the Romantic era, born in 1833 in Saint Petersburg. He was the illegitimate son of a Georgian nobleman. He was taught at home and studied at the Medical-Surgical Academy, after which he became a professor of chemistry. Music remained his second profession, which he practised in his spare time or during illness. Borodin belonged to The Five, a group of composers who wanted to write a uniquely Russian classical music. He became a pupil of Mily Balakirev.

His best-known works are his symphonies, his two string quartets, the symphonic sketch In the Steppes of Central Asia and the opera Prince Igor, with the Polovtsian Dances in it. Prince Igor remained unfinished. Rimsky-Korsakov and Alexander Glazunov completed the opera after his death. His First Symphony was first performed in 1869. Franz Liszt made sure that the symphony was also heard in Germany in 1880. Borodin died suddenly at a ball in 1887.

His music has a strong melody and rich harmonies. In 1953 the musical Kismet used his music in songs such as Stranger in Paradise, And This Is My Beloved and Baubles, Bangles, and Beads. In this way his classical work ended up in the popular music of the twentieth century.
artiest/alexander-borodin.listen: Listen to the Polovtsian Dances from Prince Igor and notice the long melodic lines and the lively rhythms, and see whether you recognise the melody from Stranger in Paradise.
